cards.definition: In C11 terminology, specified behavior is determined by the standard for the stated case. Implementation-defined behavior allows documented implementation choices. Unspecified behavior allows a set of alternatives without requiring the implementation to document which is chosen. Undefined behavior imposes no requirements on that execution. A debugger observation does not turn an unspecified choice or undefined execution into a portable guarantee.
major_error_concepts: Treating undefined behavior as a guaranteed implementation-specific result.
Saying unspecified behavior requires a documented implementation choice.
cards.prompt: In C11, distinguish specified, implementation-defined, unspecified and undefined behavior.
required_concepts: Distinguish a standard-prescribed result, documented implementation choice, undocumented permitted alternatives, and undefined behavior with no requirements.
An observed result alone does not establish a portable language guarantee.

cards.definition: A dangling pointer is a pointer associated with an object whose lifetime has ended, for example after deallocation or exit from the owning automatic-storage scope. It no longer provides valid access to that former object. In C11, such a pointer value becomes indeterminate; a remembered address or a non-null test is not a lifetime guarantee. Keeping an alias does not keep the object alive.
major_error_concepts: Defining dangling as merely having a null address.
Assuming an old alias keeps freed or out-of-scope storage alive.
cards.prompt: Define Dangling pointer. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The referenced object lifetime has ended, so the old reference no longer authorizes object access.
A retained alias or apparently non-null address does not restore the object lifetime.

cards.definition: A double free attempts to deallocate an allocation that has already been deallocated, without a new valid allocation ownership contract. In C, a repeated free of that allocation is undefined behavior; free(NULL) is a permitted no-op. A later fresh allocation may reuse an address without being the same allocation identity. Nulling one alias does not repair other stale aliases.
major_error_concepts: Calling repeated free(NULL) a double-free violation.
Freeing through a stale alias after another alias released the allocation.
cards.prompt: Define Double free. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The same allocation has already been freed; distinguish allocation identity from a reusable numeric address.
free(NULL) is a no-op, and stale aliases still require correct lifetime/ownership handling.

cards.definition: In the C11 multithreaded memory model, a data race consists of two conflicting actions in different threads on the same memory location, at least one a write and at least one non-atomic, where neither action happens before the other. major_error_concepts: Calling two correctly performed relaxed atomic stores a C11 data race solely because no cross-thread happens-before edge orders them.
Treating a genuine non-atomic data race as merely an unpredictable but otherwise defined interleaving.
cards.prompt: What is a data race in the C11 multithreaded memory model, and how does it differ from a logical race among atomic operations?
required_concepts: Conflicting different-thread accesses to one location include a write and at least one non-atomic action, with neither happens before the other.
C11 data races are undefined behavior; all-atomic operations can still have logical ordering bugs without a data race.

cards.definition: For POSIX-style regular-file reads, a nonnegative return value is the number of bytes actually read; it can be shorter than requested. For a positive request size, zero indicates the file position is at or beyond EOF at that time. A request for zero bytes can return zero without proving EOF. On error, read returns -1 with errno; process only the returned byte count and handle EINTR or would-block errors according to their contract. Other descriptor types can have additional zero-return semantics.
major_error_concepts: Treating a zero-byte read result as proof the file has no more data.
Using all requested buffer bytes after only a short count was returned.
cards.prompt: For POSIX-style regular-file read calls, interpret full/short, zero and error results, including a zero-byte request.
required_concepts: Interpret positive/short byte counts as actual progress and -1 with errno as error, not a full-buffer guarantee.
Zero indicates EOF for the specified positive-count regular-file case, but a zero-length request returning zero is not EOF evidence.

cards.definition: For a POSIX-style write, the nonnegative result reports bytes actually written and may be shorter than requested; -1 reports failure with errno. Advance by positive progress and retry only the unwritten suffix when the error/readiness policy permits. A zero-byte write to a regular file can succeed with return value zero and no data effect. An unexpected zero-progress result for pending data must not be treated as full success or retried in an uncontrolled busy loop. A successful write alone is not a durable-storage guarantee.
major_error_concepts: Retrying the whole original buffer after positive partial progress.
Claiming every successful write must return a positive count.

required_concepts: Track actual bytes written, including partial results, and retry only the remaining suffix under the error/readiness policy.
A zero-byte regular-file write may validly return zero; zero progress on pending data is not complete success.
